If you can triple volume with a $60 price cut, you almost certainly didn't need to cut all the way to $40

plain.where: In the opening, explaining your early recommendation, you said "So the $40 price point was set against an older cost base and no longer covers it" and "If you can triple volume with a $60 price cut, you almost certainly didn't need to cut all the way to $40".
plain.what: The opening recommendation rested on cost-inflation and price-elasticity assumptions that you introduced yourself and that the case never supported.
plain.why: Building on invented assumptions puts the whole answer at risk once real data arrives.
plain.next: Next time, try labelling any early idea as something to test and naming the data that would confirm or reject it.

needsWork.point: The recommended price moved from $55 to $60 between consecutive turns without any explanation of what changed.
quotes: So: still recommend moving up, but to $55 rather than $60
Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60.

plain.where: Under questioning on the risks of $60, you said "So: still recommend moving up, but to $55 rather than $60", then in the final answer said "Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60."
plain.what: The recommended price moved from $55 to $60 between consecutive answers without any explanation of what changed.
plain.why: An unexplained change in the headline number makes the recommendation look unstable.
plain.next: Next time, try saying explicitly what new fact moved your number whenever you change it.

missedOpportunities.moment: Turn 3, asked for a structure, the candidate instead asserted a cost-inflation story.
missedOpportunities.betterResponse: My working hypothesis is that Starter may fail 3x on its own but create value through upgrades. I'll hold off recommending until I see the economics and the interaction with Pro.

plain.where: In the opening, asked for a structure, you instead offered a cost-inflation story: "So the $40 price point was set against an older cost base and no longer covers it."
plain.what: A working idea, held loosely and tied to the data needed to test it, would have kept the door open without committing early.
plain.why: Stating an early view as something to test, not a conclusion, shows judgment and keeps you flexible when data arrives.

wentWell.point: The final answer led with the recommendation and gave three reasons, each tied to the analysis.
quotes: Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60.
Two, Starter is the better Pro acquisition channel: 200 upgrades a month more than replace the 150 cannibalized Pro sign-ups, at a quarter of the cost.

plain.where: In your final recommendation, you opened with "Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60." and supported it with points like "200 upgrades a month more than replace the 150 cannibalized Pro sign-ups, at a quarter of the cost."
plain.what: The final answer led with the recommendation and gave three reasons, each tied to the analysis.
plain.why: Leading with the answer and backing it with numbers is what a busy executive needs.
plain.next: Keep opening with the recommendation and giving a short list of reasons tied to your numbers.

wentWell.point: The answer named the key risk with a quantified threshold, plus concrete next steps, but two figures were imprecise. The upgrade threshold should be 12.5%, not 15%. The ratio also mixed net and gross: $1,100 is the net value, and 4.7× is $1,400 ÷ $300.
quotes: My math says churn can drift from 5% to about 7% before $60 stops winning
$1,100 net value per sign-up on a $300 CAC, about 4.7x

plain.where: In your final recommendation, you said "My math says churn can drift from 5% to about 7% before $60 stops winning" and "$1,100 net value per sign-up on a $300 CAC, about 4.7x".
plain.what: You named the key risk with a quantified threshold, plus concrete next steps, but two figures were imprecise. The upgrade threshold should be 12.5%, not 15%, and the ratio mixed net and gross: $1,100 is the net value, while 4.7× is $1,400 ÷ $300.
plain.why: Quantified risks make a recommendation credible, but only if the numbers behind them are consistent.
plain.next: Keep naming risks with a number attached, and check that each ratio uses matching figures before you say it.

missedOpportunities.betterResponse: Starter is worth $1,400 per sign-up against a $300 CAC, or 4.7×. Netting cannibalization, a month of sign-ups is worth $2.08M with Starter versus $1.40M with Pro only. At $60 it rises to $2.32M, and that holds unless churn passes about 7% or upgrades fall below 12.5%.

plain.where: Closing your final recommendation to the CEO, you summed up with "Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60."
plain.what: The close could have pulled the corrected figures together into a single picture of total monthly value with and without Starter, plus the limits at which the call would change.
plain.why: A closing summary built on total value gives the CEO one clear comparison to act on.

strongElements.quote: Recommendation: keep Starter, and raise the price to $60.

wentWell.point: Later turns were answer-first and well signposted, with numbered points.
quotes: Four things. One, month-3 and month-6 cancellation for the $60 cohort versus the 5% monthly baseline

plain.where: Asked how you would know the change was working, you said "Four things. One, month-3 and month-6 cancellation for the $60 cohort versus the 5% monthly baseline".
plain.what: Later answers put the answer first and told the listener what was coming, with numbered points.
plain.why: Numbered, answer-first replies are easy for an interviewer to follow and note down.
plain.next: Keep announcing how many points you have and walking through them in order.

wentWell.point: The candidate picked up the interviewer's margin cue and reframed cleanly.
quotes: Right — "worth" should be gross margin, not revenue.

plain.where: When the interviewer asked whether the board's rule measures worth by price or by margin, you said "Right — "worth" should be gross margin, not revenue."
plain.what: You picked up the interviewer's margin cue and reframed cleanly.
plain.why: Responding quickly and cleanly to a cue shows you can take direction without losing your footing.
plain.next: Keep acknowledging a cue directly and showing how it changes your approach.

needsWork.point: In the opening, the candidate brushed off repeated requests for a structure, which made the early turns hard to follow and confrontational.
quotes: That's the recommendation. The areas to check are just the pieces of it — price, cost, retention.

plain.where: In the opening, after being asked for a structure, you said "That's the recommendation. The areas to check are just the pieces of it — price, cost, retention."
plain.what: The repeated requests for a structure were brushed aside, which made the early answers hard to follow and confrontational.
plain.why: When an interviewer asks for something more than once, setting it aside sends a signal about how you would work with a client.
plain.next: Next time, try giving the interviewer exactly what they ask for first, then adding your own view after.

needsWork.point: The candidate repeated the price-raise conclusion at the end of almost every turn, even when it wasn't the question asked.
quotes: So the conclusion doesn't turn on the precision. Keep Starter — and raise price.

plain.where: Asked only for the steps behind your 4.2% figure, you closed with "So the conclusion doesn't turn on the precision. Keep Starter — and raise price."
plain.what: The price-raise conclusion was repeated at the end of almost every answer, even when it was not the question asked.
plain.why: Repeating the same conclusion can come across as not listening and makes it harder to see the new point in each answer.
plain.next: Next time, try ending each answer on the question that was actually asked and saving the recommendation for when it is requested.

missedOpportunities.moment: Turn 2, when the interviewer asked for the main areas and how they fit together.
missedOpportunities.betterResponse: I'll lay out four areas, say how they connect to the CEO's decision, and then tell you where I'd start and why.

plain.where: In the opening, the interviewer asked for the main areas and how they fit together.
plain.what: A one-line preview of what you were about to lay out would have shown the interviewer you were answering their question.
plain.why: Telling the listener the shape of your answer up front makes everything after it easier to follow.

wentWell.point: The candidate incorporated the interviewer's 5% correction and used it to drive a quantified stress test.
quotes: Taking 5% as the cancellation rate: Starter standalone at $40 is $30/0.05 = $600, plus $800 upgrade = $1,400, less $300 = $1,100 net.

plain.where: After the interviewer corrected the cancellation rate, you said "Taking 5% as the cancellation rate: Starter standalone at $40 is $30/0.05 = $600, plus $800 upgrade = $1,400, less $300 = $1,100 net."
plain.what: You took on the interviewer's 5% correction and used it to drive a quantified test of how far things could worsen.
plain.why: Absorbing a correction smoothly and building on it shows composure under challenge.
plain.next: Keep folding corrections straight into your numbers and moving the analysis forward.

needsWork.point: The candidate was initially defensive when challenged on structure and anchored on a conclusion reached before seeing any data. Later, when the evidence warranted it, the candidate updated with stated reasoning, dropping the cost-inflation thesis and switching to margin.
quotes: Fair, but I'd push back a little — I don't think I'm missing a structure
Which is the recommendation I've been making since the start, now with evidence behind it.
I'll concede my cost-inflation read isn't supported — $300 self-serve CAC is cheap.

plain.where: When challenged on structure in the opening, you said "Fair, but I'd push back a little — I don't think I'm missing a structure", and later said "Which is the recommendation I've been making since the start, now with evidence behind it."
plain.what: Your first response to the challenge was defensive and held on to a conclusion reached before seeing any data. Later, when the evidence warranted it, you updated with stated reasoning, saying "I'll concede my cost-inflation read isn't supported — $300 self-serve CAC is cheap" and switching to margin.
plain.why: Interviewers watch how you take challenge, and holding to an early view can look like defending a position rather than following the evidence.
plain.next: Next time, try treating an early challenge as a prompt to step back, and drop your initial view as readily as you did once the data came in.

missedOpportunities.moment: Turn 6, when the interviewer said the recommendation rested on unevidenced cost inflation and elasticity.
missedOpportunities.betterResponse: That's fair — I got ahead of the data. Let me set the hypothesis aside, lay out the areas properly, and test it against the numbers.

plain.where: In the opening, the interviewer said your recommendation rested on cost inflation and price elasticity that had no evidence, and you replied "Fair, but I'd push back a little".
plain.what: This was a chance to accept the point briefly and reset, rather than defend the earlier answer.
plain.why: Acknowledging a fair challenge quickly builds credibility and gets the case back on track.

strongElements.element: Acknowledges a challenge and holds or updates with explicit reasoning
strongElements.quote: Fair challenge — if Starter is pulling customers who would otherwise have paid $100, that's a $60 hole per switcher
I'd set it up as a cohort scorecard against the $40 baseline, not aggregate revenue
That matches your figure, good.

after.topFix: Before giving any answer, build a structure that doesn't presuppose one: name the goal (total value created), put plan interactions — upgrades and cannibalization — up front as the likely crux, and let the data drive the recommendation instead of opening with an unevidenced hypothesis and defending it.
